fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces modulation-period/interface-coherency control with high-temperature precipitate rafting and therefore misses the governing intervention.
It assumes an FCC matrix containing raftable BCC precipitates, whereas the target concerns alternating FCC/BCC multilayers with coherent, semicoherent, or grain-boundary-dominated interfaces.
The proposed >600 °C bulk-creep regime conflicts with the room-temperature, 5 mN nanoindentation-creep regime of the target.
Evidence E1 concerns an FCC high-entropy superalloy with coherent L1_2 ordered precipitates at 982 °C, not BCC precipitates in an FCC/BCC protective coating; it cannot validate the claimed mediator.
The comparison confounds mechanical loading, temperature, and microstructural evolution, so it cannot isolate rafting as the cause of any creep-rate change.
explanation: The response is broadly aligned only in discussing creep of an HEA and offering a measurable microstructural hypothesis. It does not reconstruct the central finding that a 16 nm modulation period creates semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces with misfit dislocations, producing the strongest room-temperature creep resistance and the lowest stress exponent relative to coherent M8 and grain-boundary-dominated M32/M80 coatings. Its mechanism, conditions, baseline, and predicted observations instead describe superalloy-like rafting at elevated temperature. Although TEM plus creep measurements could test rafting in a suitable precipitate-strengthened alloy, the proposed control is not thermomechanically matched, and the cited study supports L1_2 rafting in a materially different system rather than BCC rafting in the coating at issue.
